nameStory: The Queen Angelfish earns its royal name from the distinctive crown-like spot on its forehead, making it look like it's wearing a jeweled tiara. This regal marking sets it apart from other angelfish and gives it an unmistakably majestic appearance as it glides through coral reefs.
description: The Queen Angelfish is a stunning tropical marine fish with brilliant blue and yellow coloration that looks like it swam straight out of a Caribbean postcard. This warm-water species calls coral reefs home and spends its time browsing the ocean floor for food. Adults are picky eaters with a particular fondness for sponges, while juveniles have completely different coloring and work as 'cleaner fish' removing parasites from other sea creatures.

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Brilliant blue body with bright yellow fins and tail that seem to glow underwater, creating a stunning contrast that's unmistakable

idTips.label: Crown Spot
idTips.description: Distinctive dark spot ringed with blue on the forehead that looks like a royal crown - this is the key identifying feature

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Disc-like, laterally compressed body that's taller than it is long, with a graceful oval profile typical of angelfish

idTips.label: Fins
idTips.description: Long, flowing dorsal and anal fins that extend backward, giving the fish an elegant, streamer-like appearance as it swims

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Found exclusively around coral reefs in warm tropical waters, typically browsing near the ocean floor

habitat: In New England waters, Queen Angelfish are extremely rare visitors - with only one recorded observation in the region. This tropical species would only appear during unusually warm summer conditions, possibly carried north by warm currents, and would be found in the warmest nearshore waters with rocky or artificial reef structures.

seasonality.spring: Not present in New England waters during spring as temperatures are too cold for this tropical species.
seasonality.summer: The only season when a Queen Angelfish might possibly appear in New England, during the warmest water temperatures in protected bays or near warm-water outflows.
seasonality.fall: Any rare visitor would likely perish or move south as water temperatures begin to drop in early fall.
seasonality.winter: Completely absent from New England waters due to cold temperatures that would be fatal to this tropical species.

funFact: Queen Angelfish live in harems where one colorful male tends to up to four females, and they time their spawning to occur during full moons when their transparent floating eggs have the best chance of survival.
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with the Blue Angelfish, but the Queen's distinctive crown spot on the forehead is the dead giveaway - think 'crown for the queen' to remember this key difference.
contextualKnowledge: This species is also called blue angelfish, golden angelfish, or yellow angelfish in different regions, which can cause confusion since there's also a separate species specifically called the Blue Angelfish that looks very similar.
compareHints: The Queen Angelfish is distinguished from its close relative, the Blue Angelfish, primarily by the prominent crown-like spot on its forehead. While both species share similar blue and yellow coloration and body shape, only the Queen sports this distinctive 'royal crown' marking. The two species can actually interbreed where their ranges overlap, but the crown spot remains the most reliable way to tell them apart.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Blue Angelfish can be distinguished from their closest relative, the Queen Angelfish, by their uniform blue coloration throughout the body and fins.
